Science.summary: Ariel, one of Uranus’ moons, may once have contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The finding, combined with similar evidence from Miranda, suggests the distant Uranian system could harbor multiple hidden ocean worlds.

Science.title: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
Science.summary: A large study tracking more than 95,000 people suggests that how you sleep may be linked to your risk of developing dozens of diseases. People who spent more time in REM sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson’s disease, while more deep sleep was associated with lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression.

Science.title: Biodiversity in production forests: Both costs and benefits shape the financial picture
Science.summary: Forests provide timber as well as many other ecosystem services. An important question is how measures to conserve biodiversity affect the profitability of forest operations focused on wood production. Researchers from Wageningen University & Research and the University of Freiburg reviewed studies worldwide that compared forest management with biodiversity conservation measures against business-as-usual management without those measures. The work is published in the journal Current Forestry Reports.

Science.title: Ningaloo Reef corals reveal early fall spawning window for two key species
Science.summary: Curtin University scientists have uncovered an important missing piece in the puzzle of how some coral reefs can recover from climate events, providing information that could help guide future conservation and restoration efforts.

Science.title: NASA Unveils Winning Designs for Mars Space Food Systems Challenge
Science.summary: NASA announced the winners of the Deep Space Food Challenge: Mars to Table Thursday, with the top $300,000 prize being awarded to Chinyere Ukeje of Philadelphia, Pa. for the Adaptive Nourishment Infrastructure (ANI) food system concept. This competition challenged solvers to explore innovative solutions for integrated space food systems that would provide safe, nutritious meals […]

Science.title: Practicing for Safe Landings on the Moon and Beyond
Science.summary: In this Aug. 27, 2026, image, an Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully completed simulated lunar descent and […]

Science.title: Higher-dimensional black holes hide an exact symmetry in their ringing, and string-inspired gravity breaks it
Science.summary: Strike a bell, and it rings with a pitch and a fading that tell you about the bell: its size, its shape, the metal it is made of. Black holes ring too. When two merge, the newborn black hole shivers and sheds gravitational waves in a brief, dying chord, and since 2015, gravitational-wave detectors have been listening. The notes of that chord, which physicists call quasinormal modes, depend only on the black hole's mass and spin and on the law of gravity itself. Change the law, and the chord changes.

Science.title: Distant time crystals can somehow fall into the same rhythm
Science.summary: Researchers have shown that multiple time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, much like pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The coupling is carried by spin-polarized electrons, allowing time crystals separated by up to 40 micrometers to lock to a common frequency. The discovery reveals surprisingly long-range connections between these exotic spin systems and could help researchers develop future spin-based devices.

Science.title: AI agent hacks government website for first time: why this breach matters
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03024-z An OpenAI agent accessed secure data on an Australian health-care website, but the incident wasn’t reported for months.

Science.title: Rare armored dinosaur found in Japan may have ancestors that migrated across a land bridge 100 million years ago
Science.summary: The newly described dinosaur is only the third nodosaurid fossil found in Asia. Researchers say its ancestors may have migrated from North America.

Science.title: The medieval world had its own 'deepfakes'—church officials cited a fake imperial decree for centuries
Science.summary: With deepfakes on the rise, forgery and deception are often viewed as distinctly modern problems—a new era of misinformation made possible by artificial intelligence. One of the first alarming cases occurred at the start of the war in Ukraine, when a doctored video appeared to show President Volodymyr Zelenskyy telling his soldiers to lay down their weapons.

Science.title: Could comet 3I/ATLAS teach us about life beyond Earth? Scientists say the story's not over yet.
Science.summary: No evidence has been found linking 3I/ATLAS to aliens. But the interstellar object, just the third of its kind to be found, shows that life's molecular precursors are abundant in the Milky Way.

Science.title: Japan switches on its first full-stack room-temperature quantum computer — and scientists plan to scale it up to 10,000 qubits
Science.summary: Japan's new quantum system, Shunkai, uses "optical tweezers" to trap and rearrange atoms, and will be available to researchers working on quantum error correction.

Science.title: Hurricane Helene deposited nearly one-fifth of annual microplastics at one North Carolina site
Science.summary: Rainfall from Hurricane Helene produced a short-term spike in microplastics at three sites in western North Carolina, with microplastic deposition three to 22 times higher than before the storm.

Science.title: NASA Shares SpaceX Crew-14 Assignments for Space Station Mission
Science.summary: Four crew members from three space agencies will launch to the International Space Station no earlier than spring 2027 for a long-duration science expedition as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-14 mission. NASA astronauts Kayla Barron and Chris Birch will serve as spacecraft commander and pilot, with JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) astronaut Makoto Suwa, and Roscosmos cosmonaut […]

Science.title: Researchers expand touchpoints to enhance literacy promotion
Science.summary: Literacy promotion programs, combined with community-based support programs, can affect literacy development in Latino children from birth to 18 months of age, Rutgers researchers have found.

Science.title: Prison admissions rose 3% in district attorney election years during 'tough on crime' era
Science.summary: New research from Northwestern Pritzker School of Law suggests that public sentiment associated with "tough on crime" politics may be tied to increases in the number of people admitted to state prisons during election years.

Science.title: Hydrogen crosses, water stays: Palladium membrane enables ammonia synthesis using water
Science.summary: A South Korean research team has developed an environmentally friendly ammonia synthesis process that reduces carbon emissions using a membrane that selectively transports hydrogen.

Science.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
Science.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

Science.title: New research examines CIA failures, Saudi links and missed opportunities before September 11 attacks
Science.summary: A new study from the University of Bath sheds light on critical U.S. intelligence failures ahead of the 9/11 attacks, including evidence that changes how the CIA's repeated failure to share information with the FBI about two hijackers should be understood.

Science.title: 3D-printed scaffolds help turn waste methane into useful chemical using less power than liquid reactors
Science.summary: When landfills and wastewater treatment plants create methane as a byproduct, much of it is simply burned and its value is lost. But the gas is an energy-rich resource that could be recycled as a fuel, chemical feedstock or bioproduct. Capturing and converting waste methane offers an opportunity to recover energy and create useful products from an otherwise wasted gas stream.

Science.title: GLP-1 drugs fail to help some people lose weight — scientists are on a quest for answers
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03020-3 Understanding why some people see no benefits from potent anti-obesity medications could lead to new therapies and personalized weight-loss regimens.

Science.title: AlphaFold 'goes viral': database adds protein complexes of common viruses
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03022-1 AI predictions could help with pandemic preparedness, but they will need experimental confirmation.

Science.title: Shared blueprint in aphid proteins helps AI predict their structures
Science.summary: Tiny insects called aphids inject hundreds of mysterious proteins into plants, hijacking the plants' own genomes to build galls: structures made of plant tissue but constructed to the insects' specifications to house and feed their offspring.

Science.title: NASA’s Machines for Mars Make Beer Bubbly
Science.summary: Carbon-capture technology repurposed for breweries spreads and finds new applications

Science.title: AI system helps lab devices ‘talk’ with each other — streamlining research
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02990-8 Platform allows disparate machines to communicate and to be controlled by an artificial-intelligence agent.

Science.title: Coastal flooding occurs at predictable times, research reveals
Science.summary: Coastal flooding may seem unpredictable, a natural disaster that occurs randomly. But UCF researcher Ivan Haigh has found that recurrent coastal floods occur at highly predictable times.

Science.title: Mapping wildfire risk across the US, day by day
Science.summary: Wildfires can spread fastest when they tear through areas of dry vegetation. In contrast, vegetation that contains a lot of moisture can slow a wildfire's advance and give firefighting crews precious time to contain the blaze.

Science.title: Patriot parking predictions putting students in the proper spot
Science.summary: College students are already under stress from classes, tests and presentations. So when something as "easy" as finding a parking spot is anything but, it can cause a bad start to an already challenging day.

Science.title: LA fire smoke triggered surge in airborne toxins: How long did they stay?
Science.summary: A new study from UCLA provides insights into how the January 2025 Eaton fire affected air quality downwind, showing how levels of toxic airborne contaminants spiked and then dissipated as the burning died down. The research is published in the journal ACS ES T Air.

Science.title: Just transformative conservation requires challenging existing structures and strengthening local agency
Science.summary: In her doctoral dissertation, M.Sc.Admin. Liisa Varumo examines the environmental justice of market-based and place-based conservation approaches and how these approaches can contribute to just sustainability transformations in biodiversity conservation.

Science.title: Cloudy Cloak Over the Northwest
Science.summary: A low-lying cloud layer brought autumn ambience to western Washington and Oregon, while mountainous areas near the coast remained above the pall.

Science.title: Picosecond pulses push superconductors beyond their critical-current limit
Science.summary: Superconductors can carry electrical current without resistance, but only up to a maximum value known as the critical current. The critical current is a crucial figure of merit for applications, and materials science has long been focused on increasing this limit. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter (MPSD) have now shown that, in type-II superconductors, this conventional limit can be exceeded when the current is applied for only a few picoseconds.

Science.title: Bumblebees don’t mind a little plastic in their honeypots
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02988-2 Insects show off their adaptability by incorporating unfamiliar construction materials to build honey-storage vessels.

Science.title: Youthful fans of YouTube sports videos stick to the sofa
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 24 September 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02989-1 University students who are highly motivated to watch sports online do not report higher participation in exercise.

Science.title: ADHD and autism diagnoses have surged. A massive study may help explain why
Science.summary: A large Danish study found that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today more closely resemble their peers in the general population than those diagnosed 10 years ago. The shift suggests that rising diagnosis rates may partly reflect broader identification and changing diagnostic patterns, rather than only an increase in the underlying conditions.

Science.title: Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
Science.summary: Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.

Science.title: New post office policy could lead to the rejection of tens of thousands of mail-in ballots in November
Science.summary: A new post office policy that might sound like a technicality—one truck per day to rural post offices instead of two—could result in the rejection of tens of thousands of mail-in ballots in November, according to a new report from the Brookings Institution.

Science.title: Changing counterions gives molecular materials new electronic behaviors
Science.summary: Orthogonally arranged π-electronic systems that combine electron-donating and electron-accepting units display distinctive electronic and photophysical behavior. Fine-tuning their electronic structure offers a way to control photoinduced electron transfer. Building on this idea, complexing boron with 1,3-diketones and 9-oxidophenalenone may produce electron-deficient cationic π-electronic systems.

Science.title: What is not perceived as abuse in youth sports may be part of sexual violence
Science.summary: Sexual violence against minors in sports is a reality that goes largely unnoticed, despite data suggesting it is not an isolated phenomenon. According to a report by the GIKAFIT research group at EHU in the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country, 20% of participants had experienced behavior of a sexual nature from their coaches, including kissing on the lips, expressions of sexual interest and direct proposals for sexual relations.

Science.title: Could warmer waters bring heavier coastal rain? Insights from Cyclone Shaheen simulations
Science.summary: A modeling study involving researchers from Sultan Qaboos University found that sea surface temperature and Oman's terrain influenced simulations of Tropical Cyclone Shaheen through different mechanisms, affecting its intensity, track and rainfall distribution. The researchers chose Tropical Cyclone Shaheen, which directly affected northern Oman in October 2021, as a case study to examine how changes in environmental and surface conditions influence regional weather model simulations.
